cards.b: The Sultanate (1206 to 1526) built institutions that Akbar later inherited. UPSC asks about iqta, the army, revenue reforms of Alauddin, central departments and the role of ulema and nobles. Know the Sultan-wise reforms.

The Sultan was supreme head, claiming authority from the Caliph (Iltutmish was confirmed by the Abbasid caliph, 1229). Nobility: Turks, later Khaljis, Afghans and Indian Muslims. Balban developed the theory of kingship with sijda and paibos; Chihalgani (the Forty) were Iltutmish’s nobles, broken by Balban.

Wazir (finance; Diwan-i-Wizarat), Ariz-i-mamalik (army; Diwan-i-Arz), Diwan-i-Risalat (religious matters and appeals), Diwan-i-Insha (correspondence). Sadr-us-sudur headed charity. Barid-i-mumalik headed spies. Alauddin set up Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (arrears); Firoz added Diwan-i-Khairat and Diwan-i-Bandagan.

Introduced by Iltutmish: a muqti received revenue of an area (iqta) in place of salary, collected taxes, kept troops and sent surplus. Transfer every few years. Balban checked muqtis; Alauddin reduced their powers; Firoz Tughluq made iqta hereditary; Sikandar Lodi tightened accounts.

Standing army paid in cash (dagh, horse branding; chehra, soldier rolls); price control (market controls for grain, cloth, horses, slaves) under the Shahna-i-mandi; revenue measured land (masahat), one-half of produce as kharaj; tax on houses (ghari) and grazing (chari). Intermediaries (khuts, muqaddams) were curbed.

Muhammad bin Tughluq tried token coinage, moved the capital to Daulatabad (1327), raised the Doab tax; faced rebellions, and he introduced agricultural loans (taqavi). Firoz Tughluq built canals (Hisar), 300 towns, imposed jizya on Brahmins too, abolished some cesses and set up employment bureaus.

Writers like Ziauddin Barani wanted an Islamic state. Modern historians (Mohammad Habib, K. A. Nizami, Irfan Habib) note a pragmatic state that relied on zawabit (secular regulations) over sharia. Jizya was collected, but rulers rarely demanded religious conversion.

Land revenue measurement, mansabdari ancestors (dagh), Persian as court language, the rupee (tanka and silver coin by Sher Shah) and the postal system (dak chowki) all descend from the Sultanate. Modern terms like “Diwan” and “Pargana” remain.
